reason: Seawater can enter seafloor fractures, starting the circulation loop described in the goal.
expectation: Seawater will move down into the fractured rock.

effect: The accumulating early sea has no available combinations, so I need another starting point for the circulation loop.
reaction: I was surprised that the sea itself could not be used.
reason: Inspecting the fractures should identify what can enter them or otherwise start the loop.
expectation: The report will show an available partner for the fractures, possibly seawater.

alternatives.reason: The mineral-bearing sea might be the usable seawater, but checking the fractures avoids another blind guess.

effect: The mineral-bearing sea enters the fractures, starting the circulation loop.
reaction: The automatic combination resolved which sea was usable.
reason: Seawater circulating through the crust should encounter the hot rock beneath the seafloor.
expectation: The seawater will heat as it moves through the rock.

effect: The seawater is now heated inside the crust; it may next react with the surrounding rock before rising.
reaction: The role of pressure in keeping hot fluid below the surface is interesting.
reason: Inspecting the heated water will reveal its next available route without guessing whether heating or rock reactions come next.
expectation: The report will identify a partner that advances the hydrothermal circulation.

alternatives.reason: Further contact with rock might release minerals, but its availability is uncertain.

effect: The heated water reacted with rock and now carries dissolved material, positioning it to return to the sea.
reaction: The distinction between heating the water and its subsequent chemical exchange was useful.
reason: Cooler seawater could mix with the hydrothermal fluid and help minerals precipitate at a vent, though the next step is uncertain.
expectation: The inspection will identify how the fluid rises or interacts with seawater.

alternatives.reason: Mixing with cooler seawater could produce a mineral deposit, but the fluid may need to rise first.

effect: The mineral-bearing fluid is rising through fractures, completing the return route toward the seafloor.
reaction: It is useful to see that entry and return can occur through different fractures.
reason: The returning hot fluid should encounter cooler seawater at the vent, potentially depositing minerals.
expectation: The hot fluid will mix with seawater, returning to the sea and possibly forming a mineral deposit.

effect: Mixing with cooler seawater caused minerals to precipitate, suggesting the vent deposit is forming.
reaction: The cooling-driven precipitation makes the deposit’s origin clear.
reason: Inspecting the precipitating minerals should reveal how to build the deposit or complete the fluid’s return.
expectation: The inspection will identify the next available step toward the vent deposit.

effect: Repeated precipitation built a mineral deposit around the outlet, completing the vent-deposit goal.
reaction: The modest deposit is a useful contrast to assuming every vent forms a tall chimney.
reason: The heated fluid still needs to return to the sea; inspecting it should reveal the available route.
expectation: The inspection will identify a partner that lets the fluid emerge into the sea.

effect: The hot fluid emerged into the sea as a hydrothermal plume, completing the circulation goal and the chapter.
reaction: The distinction between suspended minerals and smoke was a useful clarification.

mostWorthwhile.text: Following heated water through chemical exchange with rock made the hydrothermal process understandable, rather than just presenting a finished vent.

leastWorthwhile.text: The initial attempt with the accumulating sea was unproductive because that sea had no available combinations.

surprise.text: The usable starting point was the mineral-bearing sea, not the accumulating sea; later, the accumulating sea became usable for the returning fluid.

arbitrary.text: Having two differently named versions of the sea, only one of which could enter the fractures, felt like a naming constraint rather than an obvious physical distinction.

continue.text: Yes. The circulation loop and mineral precipitation offered a clear, useful account of a natural process, and I would be curious to see another process explained similarly.
